opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most revealing things you can study, actually. When you watch people solve ARC tasks, especially when you ask them to think aloud, what you see is not brute-force enumeration over a space of programs. Nobody sits there trying a thousand candidate transformations. Instead, they look at the grids and immediately start *describing* them: "there are objects here, this one is bigger, these two are touching, the color seems to depend on size." That description comes first, and it's what makes the search tractable.

So the way I'd frame it is that there are really two layers. There's the descriptive model, your perception of the task in terms of a vocabulary of abstractions: objects, symmetry, counting, containment, contact, goal-directedness, all these core knowledge priors. Then there's the program search, which operates *over* that description rather than over raw pixels. The description massively narrows the space. It's essentially a learned, intuitive prior telling you which few programs are even worth considering.

And what's striking is that humans typically only try a handful of hypotheses, often just one or two, before landing on the right one. That tells you the heavy lifting is done by the quality of the representation, not by the breadth of the search. If your description of the problem is good, the program almost falls out of it. If it's bad, no amount of search will save you, because the combinatorial explosion kills you.

This is precisely where I think pure discrete program synthesis approaches struggle, and also where pure deep learning approaches struggle, just from the opposite side. Discrete search has the right structure, compositional and verifiable, but no intuition guiding it, so it explodes. Deep learning has the intuition, the pattern-matching fast perception, but it can't reliably compose novel programs on the fly. The human solver is doing both at once: type 1 intuition to build the descriptive model and propose candidates, and type 2 deliberate reasoning to verify and refine.

So for me the lesson is that the path forward is a hybrid: using learned, continuous models to guide discrete program search, to produce the descriptions and the search heuristics, and then using explicit symbolic composition to actually construct and check the solution. The descriptive model is not a nice-to-have; it's the thing that makes intelligence efficient. And efficiency, how much you can do with how little experience and how little compute, is really what intelligence is about.

r001.rationale: It says human solvers first describe grids using abstractions such as objects, then search over those descriptions.

r002.rationale: It mentions a color seeming to depend on size, but does not identify causal relationships as a particular focus of human grid descriptions.

r003.rationale: It says the descriptive model “massively narrows” the program space and makes search tractable.

r004.rationale: It says that with a good description, “the program almost falls out of it,” suggesting modeling can leave very little need for search.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the human solving process is actually the strongest piece of evidence we have that program synthesis, in the classical sense, is not what's going on. When you watch someone solve an ARC task, they don't enumerate candidate programs. They look at the grids and almost immediately form a description of what they're seeing: there are objects here, this one is a container, this one is noise, the output seems to be the input with something filled in. That description comes first, and it comes fast. Only afterward do they start articulating a precise procedure, and often that procedure is just a direct readout of the description they already have.

So the descriptive model is doing most of the work. It's collapsing the search space before any search happens. If you have the right description, the space of plausible programs is tiny, maybe a handful of candidates, and you can verify them against the demonstration pairs almost trivially. If you have the wrong description, no amount of search will save you, because the primitives you're composing don't carve the problem at its joints.

This matters for how we should build systems. The purely discrete approach, where you search over a DSL with some fixed set of primitives, hits a combinatorial wall very quickly. The purely neural approach, where you train a model to map inputs to outputs directly, tends to memorize surface patterns and fails on anything genuinely novel. The interesting middle ground is using a learned model to produce the description, which is really a prior over programs, and then using a small amount of discrete search to resolve the remaining ambiguity and verify. That's much closer to what humans do. The perception system proposes, and a deliberate, symbolic process disposes.

What I find striking is that the human description is itself compositional and abstract. People don't describe the task in terms of pixels. They describe it in terms of objects, relations, symmetries, counts, goals. Those are the primitives of a very good DSL, and we didn't engineer them, they came from a lifetime of interacting with a physical world that has objects and persistence and causality. ARC was designed to lean on exactly those core knowledge priors and nothing else, which is why the puzzles feel easy to us and are hard for systems that don't have that descriptive vocabulary.

So the lesson, I think, is that the quality of the program search is almost entirely downstream of the quality of the representation you're searching in. The hard part isn't the search. The hard part is learning to see the problem the right way.

r001.rationale: The response says people quickly describe the grid in terms of objects and other features before articulating a procedure or searching programs.

r002.rationale: It mentions causality among the priors people gain from interacting with the physical world, but does not identify causal relationships as a particular focus of their descriptions of ARC grids.

r003.rationale: It says a good description collapses the search space, leaving only a handful of plausible programs.

r004.rationale: It suggests that the right description can reduce plausible programs to a handful and make verification nearly trivial, leaving only a small amount of search.

astra-6.text:
I think it suggests that program search is guided by how you describe the problem. When a human looks at an ARC task, they don’t start enumerating arbitrary programs over pixels. They form a description: there are a few objects, one of them is repeated, perhaps a color indicates which object you should move. That description makes certain operations relevant and makes most other operations irrelevant.

So a descriptive model can be very useful without itself being an executable solution. It gives you a vocabulary in which the solution becomes easy to express. If you represent the input as a flat grid of colors, the transformation might look complicated. If you represent it as objects with relationships, it might be something like, ‘Move this object inside that container.’

Of course, the initial description can be wrong. You try to construct a program, check whether it explains the examples, and revise your interpretation when it fails. So I would think of it as an interaction between forming abstractions and searching for programs. The description constrains the search, and the search gives you feedback about whether you have the right description.

r001.rationale: It says people first form a description of the task, such as identifying objects and their relationships, before constructing a program.

r002.rationale: It mentions object relationships, but does not identify causal relationships as a focus of the descriptive model.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says the description constrains the search and makes some operations relevant while excluding most others.

r004.rationale: It presents modeling and program search as interacting, but does not suggest extensive modeling could nearly eliminate the need for search.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it suggests that program search is heavily guided by how you describe the problem in the first place. When you look at an ARC puzzle, you don't immediately enumerate programs. You see objects, boundaries, repetitions, symmetries. You might say, “This object is missing a piece,” or, “These examples show the same shape moving.” That description makes certain transformations natural candidates and makes most other transformations irrelevant.

So a descriptive model doesn't necessarily give you the solution, but it gives you a useful space in which to search for one. And the process is iterative: you form an interpretation, try a transformation, check it against the examples, and revise your interpretation if it doesn't work.

The important point is that the representation itself is part of what you have to discover. If you fix the representation in advance and only search over programs expressed in that representation, you may make a very simple solution extremely difficult to find. Human solving suggests that discovering the right abstractions and finding the program are closely coupled.

r001.rationale: It says solvers first see objects, boundaries, repetitions, and symmetries before enumerating programs, and form interpretations of the grid.

r002.rationale: It discusses objects and visual patterns, but does not identify causal relationships as a focus of the descriptive model.

r003.rationale: It says the description creates a useful search space, making some transformations natural and others irrelevant.

r004.rationale: It does not suggest modeling could nearly eliminate program search; it says the model guides search and is revised through testing.
